content:
Getting up at night when stiff, sleepy and in the dark can be risky. For some people, a bedside commode makes night-time toileting safer.

This guide explains options and safe use. It is educational information, not a personal assessment.

Is a commode right for you?

  • You need the toilet often at night.
  • The walk to the toilet is long, or involves stairs.
  • You feel unsteady or stiff when you first get up.
  • You have fallen at night before.

Choosing and using a commode

  • An OT can advise on height, armrests and whether it needs to be wheeled.
  • Place it on a non-slip surface with brakes on, if fitted.
  • Use a night light.
  • Make sure there is a way to call for help.

Other ways to reduce night-time risk

  • Sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before standing.
  • Keep a walking aid within reach.
  • A urinal bottle may be an alternative for some people.
  • Ask your GP about frequent night-time urination, as there may be a treatable cause.

Getting a commode

Ask your GP or council for an occupational therapy assessment. Community equipment services may loan commodes. Short-term loans may also be available from charities.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Can I get a commode free?

Many areas loan them after an OT assessment.

Is it embarrassing?

Many people use them, and they can be discreet.
